answer: Part of this is true. The US has given Israel about $174 billion in current dollars, the largest cumulative total since World War II (Egypt: over $90 billion, historical dollars). Under a 2016 agreement the US pledged $38 billion for 2019 to 2028: $3.3 billion a year in military grants and $500 million a year for missile defence. It is a pledge; Congress votes each year. In April 2024 Congress appropriated $3.5 billion in grants and $5.2 billion for missile defence, in a $95 billion package that gave Ukraine $60.8 billion. In the war's first year, Brown's Costs of War project counts at least $17.9 billion in approved security assistance, a partial figure. Left out: estimates of US aid's share of Israel's defence budget run from under 8 to about 20 percent. On 3 November 2026 President Trump said the aid would stop by year end; Congress controls the money.

could_not_verify: A single audited figure for US arms actually delivered since October 2023: the $17.9 billion is the Costs of War project's count of approved assistance and the authors call it partial; the AP says full shipments cannot be tracked as Ukraine's can.
The Israeli Ministry of Defense statement of 90,000 tons: the original and the Times of Israel article could not be fetched; it is quoted via the CRS report and the CFR.

Fact 1 (largest cumulative recipient) now has the CFR (with the local news report that repeats it, counted as one), USAFacts and Ynetnews. I did not find a Brookings or Carnegie explainer or a readable ForeignAssistance.gov page.

Fact 2 (Egypt and Ukraine): the Egypt total rests on the CRS (government) and Al Jazeera, which reports a lower figure (more than $87 billion, February 2025); I found no State Department or foreign-assistance data page for Egypt that I could read. Ukraine rests on the CFR and NPR. The CRS Israel and Egypt totals use historical dollars; the CFR Ukraine figure counts war-related spending, including US operations in Europe, so it is not like-for-like.
Congress's reaction to the 3 November 2026 announcement, and whether any funding has changed; the pages read are from the day it was announced.
Whether $26.4 billion (CBS) or $26 billion (VOA) is the right total for Israel-related items in the April 2024 law; the card gives the law's line items instead.

Whether the 3 November 2026 announcement is more than a statement: Al Jazeera says it was not clear what form of aid Trump meant, and TWZ quotes Politico that no formal document was submitted by the prime minister's office. Fact 6 and the last sentence of the answer say only what he said, and rest on three independent outlets (TWZ, Al Jazeera, Reuters via Al-Monitor), all reporting one television interview.

Still short of three independent reliable sources: fact 5 only (the $17.9 billion). Fact 5 is worded as one study's figure; the CFR's $16.3 billion is a different measure, not a second tally of the same thing.
The case for the aid on this card rests on one senator (via the Times of Israel) and one 2016 White House statement; a strategist or scholar who makes it was not read for this card.
Round three: the AP item on the $17.9 billion reports the Costs of War project's figure, so both are declared one source ('wire': 'Costs of War'); no second tally of approved aid was found.
not_claimed: This card does not say the aid is right or wrong, or that it should continue.
It does not say that any specific US-made weapon caused any specific death; that is a question for the incident-level records.
It does not say the aid pays for the whole of Israel's war; it gives amounts and the share of the Israeli defence budget that two sources report (about 14 to 20 percent before the war).
It does not say Congress or the president has decided the future of the aid after November 2026.

answer_claims.says: The US has given Israel about $174 billion in current dollars, the largest cumulative total since World War II (Egypt: over $90 billion, historical dollars).
Under a 2016 agreement the US pledged $38 billion for 2019 to 2028: $3.3 billion a year in military grants and $500 million a year for missile defence.
It is a pledge; Congress votes each year.
In April 2024 Congress appropriated $3.5 billion in grants and $5.2 billion for missile defence, in a $95 billion package that gave Ukraine $60.8 billion.
In the war's first year, Brown's Costs of War project counts at least $17.9 billion in approved security assistance, a partial figure.
Left out: estimates of US aid's share of Israel's defence budget run from under 8 to about 20 percent.
On 3 November 2026 President Trump said the aid would stop by year end; Congress controls the money.

skeptic.notes: Round three (the last). Changed since round two: the defence-budget fact now has CFR, INSS (a paper written after June 2018, 'almost a fifth') and Al-Monitor ('less than eight percent of the projected 2026 budget'), all read, three independent estimates, and the answer says 'estimates run from under 8 to about 20 percent'; a senator (Lindsey Graham, Jewish Insider) is quoted on aid serving American interests; the CRS report is cited from EveryCRSReport and every figure I rechecked is there ($174bn to date, 14 percent with the Jane's note, $38bn/$33bn/$5bn, $3.5bn, $5.2bn, $769.3m, 90,000 tons, over $90bn for Egypt). Still blocking: fact 1 (largest recipient: CFR, and WJLA which repeats the CFR; it is a claim about the world, so the record flag does not apply unless reworded as 'the CRS reports...', and then needs two sources reporting it independently), fact 2 (Egypt figure: the CRS only; Ukraine: CFR and NPR), and fact 5 (the $17.9bn is one dataset repeated by AP; I declared them one source, leaving two). Person: for fact 1 find a second independent statement of 'largest recipient' (e.g. a Brookings, Carnegie or news explainer that does not cite the CFR); for fact 2 a second source for Egypt's cumulative total (e.g. the State Department's foreign assistance data or a news explainer); for fact 5 a second tally of approved aid since 7 October (e.g. a news analysis by Reuters or Responsible Statecraft's own count).

citer.notes: Round three: the answer changed in two places and answer_claims were redone: the defence-budget sentence now says estimates run from under 8 to about 20 percent (fact 3), and 'It is a pledge, not a law' became 'It is a pledge' (fact 0 says 'subject to congressional appropriation'; the 'not a law' half rested only on the rescission-era wording of fact 6). Every sentence ties to the facts.
